The table lists the nodes at each coreness value." width="100%"} The k-core is the maximal subgraph where every node has degree >= k. A node's coreness is the highest k-value for which it belongs to the k-core. Uses iterative pruning: repeatedly removes nodes with degree < k until all remaining nodes have degree >= k. Higher coreness indicates nodes in denser, more cohesive parts of the graph. The k-core decomposition is useful for finding the 'nucleus' of a network. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store coreness values. If `None`, uses `coreness` as the attribute name. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to coreness values. If `False`, stores values as node attributes and returns the Graph for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int] or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: Dictionary mapping node IDs to coreness values (non-negative integers). If `return_dict=` is `False`: Returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node in a complete graph K4 is connected to all three others, so removing any one node still leaves a fully-connected triangle behind -- meaning all four nodes share the maximum possible coreness of `3`: ::: {#9457e3cd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D")]) ) graph.coreness(return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {3: 3, 1: 3, 4: 3, 2: 3} ``` ::: :::
